sheet-1-1.description: The main part of sheet 1 shows the Passaic River front of Harrison between Middlesex Street on the west and Sussex Street on the east, from the river south to South 1st Street at the bottom edge. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned so that north points to the right. The part is industrial. On the west the Marine Engine and Machine Company occupies a large steel-framed machine shop with smithing, brazing, casting and pattern buildings; the tracks of the Pennsylvania Railroad freight line run down Railroad Avenue, lettered as 116 feet wide, beside it. Between Railroad Avenue and Essex Street stands the Headley and Farmer Company, manufacturers of trunks, travelling bags and suit cases, in a group of mill, finishing and storage buildings with a lumber form on the river. East of Essex Street are the National Oil and Supply Company warehouse, then being built, and the Standard Bitulithic Company plant, and a curving railroad siding crosses the blocks toward Bergen Street. Between Bergen and Sussex streets the lots are empty except for a platform beside the tracks along South 1st Street. Fire protection notes for the two large works are printed in the upper left. The heavy line at the top separates this part from the riverfront strip west of Middlesex Street drawn above it.
notes: Placed from three junctions along South 1st Street only (helmert); low confidence.
Railroad Avenue survives as New Jersey Railroad Avenue but its drawn centre does not match the modern way; left out.
Middlesex Street no longer exists under that name; the riverfront has been redeveloped.

50 ft, north to the right. Two parts split by a heavy line: part 1 (lower, main) riverfront Middlesex to Sussex south to S. 1st St (Marine Engine & Machine Co., Headley & Farmer Co.), helmert along S. 1st St; part 2 (upper strip) riverfront Monmouth to Middlesex north of S. 1st St (Commercial Acetylene Co., Passaic River Yacht Club), no surviving junction, placed from four points on S. 1st St carried from sheet 4 (helmert).

sheet-1-2.description: The upper strip of sheet 1, above the heavy dividing line, shows the Passaic River front of Harrison between Monmouth Street on the west and Middlesex Street on the east, from the river bank south to South 1st Street, which runs along the bottom of the strip with the tops of the blocks beyond it. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned so that north points to the right, like the rest of the sheet. The strip continues the blocks shown on sheet 4 across South 1st Street. Burlington, Hunterdon and Somerset Streets run from South 1st Street toward the river, which cuts diagonally across the strip, so that the blocks are deep near Middlesex Street and shallow near Monmouth Street. Most lots are vacant and only subdivided. Block 75, between Hunterdon and Somerset Streets, holds the Commercial Acetylene Company: a long storage and charging building on Hunterdon Street with generator, compressor and electric motor rooms, an acetone boiler house, an oil house, a testing room, an office and a round gas holder. At the river end of Somerset Street stands the club house of the Passaic River Yacht Club on its pier. Block 74, on Middlesex Street, carries buildings of the Marine Engine and Machine Company, whose main works are drawn on the lower part of this sheet: storage sheds, a paint storage, an oil house and a machine and wood-working shop with a hose cart house. A few small buildings stand in block 76, and block 77 at Monmouth Street is empty. A dashed line marks the bulkhead or pier line in the river.
notes: Placed from four points on South 1st Street carried from sheet 4 (block corners drawn on both sheets), as a similarity (helmert); no surviving junction lies in the strip. Medium-low confidence away from South 1st Street.
Hunterdon and Monmouth Streets no longer exist; Middlesex Street is today Angelo Cifelli Drive south of the river front.
Commercial Acetylene Company works with gas holder in block 75.

50 ft, north to the right. Two parts split by a heavy line: part 1 (lower, main) riverfront Middlesex to Sussex south to S. 1st St (Marine Engine & Machine Co., Headley & Farmer Co.), helmert along S. 1st St; part 2 (upper strip) riverfront Monmouth to Middlesex north of S. 1st St (Commercial Acetylene Co., Passaic River Yacht Club), no surviving junction, placed from four points on S. 1st St carried from sheet 4 (helmert).

sheet-2-1.description: The main part of sheet 2 shows the Harrison riverfront between Sussex Street and Harrison Avenue, from the Passaic River south to South 1st Street at the bottom edge, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned so that north points to the right. Dey Street crosses the middle of the part, and Passaic Avenue leaves Harrison Avenue near the bridge approach. The riverbank is lined with lumber yards: E. W. McClave and Son's sawing and planing mill with its heavy lumber sheds, and J. J. Spurr and Sons, cut stone contractors, with a large stone cutting shed and a storage shed being built. South of Dey Street stands the patent leather works of H. Hahn and Stumpf, with finishing, japanning, tanning and storage buildings and a sunning platform. Along South 1st Street lies the Pennsylvania Railroad freight yard with an iron-clad freight house, platforms and a curving spur that runs north across Warren Street to the lumber yards. A row of stores, flats and a chemical laboratory and express office line Harrison Avenue near the bridge. Across the river at the top the City of Newark is indicated, with the draw bridge carrying Harrison Avenue over the Passaic. The area above the heavy diagonal line at the upper left is a separate inset and is not part of this description.
notes: Jersey Street / South 1st Street and Dey Street / Warren Street left out: the modern nodes lie 7 to 15 m from the drawn junctions (Dey and Jersey realigned at their west ends).
H. Hahn and Stumpf patent leather works; J. J. Spurr and Sons cut stone works; E. W. McClave and Son planing mill.

50 ft, north to the right. Part 1 (main) riverfront Sussex to Harrison Av, Dey St, S. 1st St, Penna RR freight yard (J.J. Spurr & Sons, H. Hahn & Stumpf). Part 2: inset above the heavy diagonal line, Walker Chemical Works on Harrison Av at Frank Creek (Kearny), no street junction: unplaced.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: Walker Chemical Works, Harrison Avenue at Frank Creek (Kearny) (no street junction; Frank Creek is not in the reference data; needs a surveyed point at the Harrison Avenue crossing of Frank Creek).

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3 covers the western tip of Harrison on the east bank of the Passaic River, which here bends in a wide curve; the opposite bank is lettered as the City of Newark, with a reference to Volume Three, and Jackson Street crosses to it on a bridge at the lower left. Unlike the neighbouring sheets, this one is drawn at 100 feet to an inch, with north toward the right. The drawn area is a grid of long narrow blocks, numbered 78 to 81, 104 to 113, 139 to 143, 147 and 148, laid out in rows of unbuilt lots between South 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th Streets, and cross streets named Cape May, Cumberland, Salem, Gloucester and Monmouth, each marked 60 feet wide. Almost all of the lots are empty. The exceptions are on the river side and in the north. Block 106 belongs to the Public Service Corporation of New Jersey and holds a large gasometer, and block 107 holds two oil tanks. The Otto Coke Co. has a coke storage shed and an iron-clad building on block 109 beside the river. A valve house stands on the river bank near South 3rd Street. The Pennsylvania Railroad tracks cross the top right corner on a diagonal and cut across blocks 80, 81, 104 and 105. A large unsubdivided tract at the bottom of the sheet is lettered Canada Farm. A compass rose and the scale bar are at the lower left. The edges of sheets 4, 7 and 9 are numbered in the right margin.
notes: Drawn at 100 feet to an inch, unlike most sheets of the atlas.
Cape May is the only street still present; modern Cape May Street meets Frank E. Rodgers Boulevard South (old South 4th Street) at the drawn junction.
Cumberland, Salem, Gloucester and Monmouth no longer exist; the area is now Red Bull Arena and the Harrison waterfront.
Control is one detected junction plus block corners carried from sheets 4 and 7 along the right edge, so the fit is weak away from that edge.
Public Service Corporation of New Jersey gasometer on block 106; Otto Coke Co. on block 109.

100 ft, north to the right. West tip of Harrison on the Passaic River: S. 2nd to 5th Sts, Cape May to Monmouth; gasometer, Otto Coke Co. One detected junction plus three points carried from sheets 4 and 7.

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 shows eight blocks in the west end of Harrison, near the Passaic River, bounded by South 1st Street at the top and South 3rd Street at the bottom, with north toward the right. Monmouth, Burlington, Hunterdon, Somerset and Middlesex Streets run across the sheet between the block columns, each marked 60 feet wide. The blocks are numbered 82 to 85 in the upper row and 100 to 103 in the lower row, and are cut into long narrow lots, most of them vacant. Building is concentrated in a few places. Block 83 holds a group of frame dwellings, flats and tenements, and a vacant, dilapidated brick building at its upper end. Block 85 carries the Marine Engineering and Machine Co. pattern storage, an iron-clad building of three storeys with a reference to sheet 1, and below it a storage yard with oil tanks of the Diamond Compound Co. Block 100 has dwellings and tenements, junk yards, a hall and a row of dwellings along Middlesex Street. Block 103 at the left is cut diagonally by the Pennsylvania Railroad, whose tracks cross the lower left corner. A compass rose and the Passaic River appear at the upper left, and the six-inch water pipe is drawn along the top edge. A scale bar and the sheet numbers of neighbouring sheets 1, 3, 5 and 7 are in the margins.
notes: Middlesex is today's Angelo Cifelli Drive (the fit places the modern line on the drawn street).
South 1st and 2nd Streets keep their names today; South 3rd Street here is 3rd Street south of New Jersey Railroad Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
Monmouth, Burlington, Hunterdon and Somerset streets mostly no longer exist; only Burlington Street and part of Somerset Street remain in the modern data.
Control is detected junctions on Burlington and Middlesex plus parcel block corners; the Marine Engineering and Machine Co. building is also drawn on sheet 1.
50 ft, north to the right. Blocks 82-85, 100-103 between S. 1st and S. 3rd Sts, Monmouth to Middlesex (Middlesex = Angelo Cifelli Drive); 4 junctions and 6 parcel block corners.

sheet-5.description: Sheet 5 covers the area north of sheet 8 in the west end of Harrison, from South 1st Street at the top to South 3rd Street at the bottom, with north toward the right. Middlesex, Essex, Bergen and Sussex Streets cross it, and Railroad Avenue, drawn 116 feet wide, runs through the left part with the Pennsylvania Railroad freight line. Essex Street and Bergen Street are lettered 60 feet wide. The blocks are numbered 86 to 89 above South 2nd Street and 96 to 99 below it. The upper left holds the large pink brick foundry and shops of the Marine Engine and Machine Co., the Diamond Compound Co. lubricating oils works, and a line of dwellings and flats beside Railroad Avenue. In block 88 is the J. K. Osborne Mfg. Co. metal novelties factory and the Graff, Regen and Cooke forge and structural iron and steel works, with a watchman, steam heat and electric light listed in the notes. Blocks 87 and 89 hold rows of dwellings on the street frontages, and block 98 a few dwellings and a tenement. Most lots in blocks 96 to 99 are vacant. A dense group of sidings and spur tracks lies between Essex and Bergen Streets, and the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western tracks cut the lower right corner. A compass rose is placed at South 2nd Street and Bergen Street, and the scale bar at the bottom.
notes: Middlesex is today's Angelo Cifelli Drive; Railroad Avenue is New Jersey Railroad Avenue, whose modern line lies about 15 m west of the drawn avenue and was not used.
Fitted scale is about 1.5 percent smaller than the other sheets of the atlas.
Control is detected junctions on Essex, Bergen and Sussex plus parcel block corners on blocks 99, 87 and 89.
Marine Engine and Machine Co. is the building drawn on sheet 4 as Marine Eng. and Mach. Co.
50 ft, north to the right. Middlesex to Sussex, S. 1st to S. 3rd Sts; Railroad Av; Marine Engine and Machine Co., J. K. Osborne. Fitted scale 1.6 percent under the atlas value.

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 covers the blocks of central Harrison between South 1st Street at the top and South 3rd Street at the bottom, with Sussex Street on the left, Warren Street and Jersey Street crossing the middle, and Harrison Avenue running down the right-hand side. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and is turned so that north lies toward the right of the page. A wide band of railroad right-of-way crosses it diagonally from lower left to upper right: the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western tracks with a passenger station, platforms, a steel bridge, passages and retaining walls, with a footbridge near the avenue. The upper left holds the Fairlie and Wilson Coal Company's coal pockets, a long raised structure with tracks above it on the left, together with wood and coal sheds, a coal pile, a wood pile and rag storage buildings, and the company's stables and a harness works of C. S. Osborne and Company in the block below. The blocks along South 1st Street and Harrison Avenue are lined with frame stores and saloons, flats, a laundry, drug store, hardware stores and a bakery. The Parker Bruen Manufacturing Company, with its power and heating plant, stands beside Jersey Street, and a parochial school and a row of apartments occupy blocks near South 3rd Street. A fire alarm box is marked on Harrison Avenue. Water pipes of 6 and 8 inches run in the streets, hydrants are numbered, and the street widths are lettered (60 and 66 feet). A compass rose sits in the margin by South 2nd Street. Adjoining sheets 2, 11, 17 and 18 are indicated at the edges, and the blocks are numbered 90 to 95.
notes: The street names on this sheet (South 1st, 2nd and 3rd Streets, Sussex, Warren, Jersey) are the modern South 1st Street, South 2nd Street, South 3rd Street, Sussex Street, Warren Street and Jersey Street.
Jersey Street / South 1st Street was hand-picked; Harrison Avenue / South 1st Street and Jersey Street / South 2nd Street (inside the railroad right-of-way) were left out of the control.
The sheet is turned with north to the right (rotation about 93 degrees).
50 ft, north to the right. S. 1st to S. 3rd Sts, Sussex to Harrison Av; D L & W station and tracks, Holy Cross school.

sheet-7.description: Sheet 7 lies south of sheet 4 in the west end of Harrison, from South 3rd Street at the top to South 5th Street at the bottom, with north toward the right. It is cut diagonally from the upper left to the lower right by the Pennsylvania Railroad main line, with the Harrison station, a freight house and platforms between block 115 and the tracks. The blocks above South 4th Street are numbered 114 to 117 and are cut into narrow vacant lots. Below it, blocks 138, 137, 135 and 136 form the Monmouth, Burlington, Hunterdon and Somerset columns, and the larger part of the area is open ground. B. M. Shanley's Sons Co., contractors, occupy a storage yard with sheds and a spur siding on blocks 137 and 138. At the right, block 134 holds the Reuther Bros. iron foundry, pattern shop and machine shop and the Hyatt Roller Bearing Co. works, which is marked as having a watchman clock with thirteen stations and fire pails distributed. Dwellings and a saloon front Middlesex Street at the right edge. The compass rose sits near the centre, a scale bar and the edge of sheet 9 are along the bottom, and edges of sheets 3, 4 and 8 are marked on the other sides.
notes: South 4th Street is today's Frank E. Rodgers Boulevard South; Middlesex is Angelo Cifelli Drive.
Somerset Street's modern line lies about 10 m east of the drawn street and its junctions were left out of the control.
Monmouth, Burlington and Hunterdon streets no longer exist.
The South 4th Street label is partly hidden by railroad lines; read as South 4th Street.
Placed by block corners carried from sheet 4 along South 3rd Street and parcel block corners along South 4th Street; no street junction was detected.

50 ft, north to the right. S. 3rd to S. 5th Sts, Monmouth to Middlesex; PRR main line, Hyatt Roller Bearing. No detected junction: placed from points carried from sheet 4 and parcel block corners on S. 4th St. Modern Somerset St about 10 m off the drawn street.

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8 shows part of western Harrison from South 3rd Street at the top to South 5th Street at the bottom, with north toward the right and South 4th Street crossing the middle. Middlesex, Railroad Avenue, Essex, Bergen and Sussex Streets run across the sheet. Railroad Avenue is drawn 116 feet wide and carries Pennsylvania Railroad freight tracks, and the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad main line crosses the sheet diagonally, with a coal pockets and a car shed on its west side. Essex and Bergen Streets are marked 60 feet wide. The Driver-Harris Wire Co. works fills block 118 at the upper left, and the National Ventilating Co. and Walsh's Sons and Co., junk dealers, occupy block 133 below. At the right is the Webb Folding Box Co. factory, with a notice of watchman, steam heat and electric light, and below South 4th Street the large pink General Electric Company works, covering blocks 130 and 131 and linked by an iron-clad bridge across Bergen Street. The Semi-Dry Battery Co. stands at South 5th Street. Rows of flats and dwellings face South 4th Street and the north side of block 121. A compass rose is placed at South 4th Street and Railroad Avenue. A scale bar is at the bottom.
notes: South 4th Street is today's Frank E. Rodgers Boulevard South; Middlesex is Angelo Cifelli Drive; Railroad Avenue is New Jersey Railroad Avenue.
The modern Essex Street is realigned south of South 4th Street; the junction with South 5th Street was matched on the drawn street.
Control lies in the eastern half; the left (Middlesex, Railroad Avenue) side has none, so the placement there is weaker.
Driver-Harris Wire Co. is the firm named on block 118; General Electric Company is also drawn on sheet 10 (See Sheet No. 8).
50 ft, north to the right. S. 3rd to S. 5th Sts, Middlesex to Sussex; Driver-Harris, Webb Folding Box, General Electric. Control only in the eastern half.

sheet-9-1.description: The main part of sheet 9 covers the west end of Harrison between South 5th Street on the west and South 7th Street on the east, from Middlesex Street at the top south to Monmouth Street and block 148 at the bottom. Unlike the neighbouring sheets 7, 8 and 10 it is drawn with north up, at 50 feet to an inch. The western half, blocks 148 to 152 between South 5th and South 6th Streets, is filled by the Crucible Steel Company of America, Atha Works, whose plant has closed the cross streets there: the iron-clad main mill building with its rolls and furnaces, the wire mill and ten-inch mill, three numbered hammer shops, machine and tempering shops, pickling and tapping rooms, gas producers, a pump house with a water purifier on an elevated platform, offices, a laboratory, pattern storage and a warehouse, with a watchman and fire-protection note. Railroad sidings and coal pockets fan out across the works from the Pennsylvania Railroad main line, which crosses the top left corner. East of South 6th Street the blocks 170 to 174 are laid out along Somerset, Hunterdon and Burlington Streets; further shops of the works, the melting furnaces, mixing and shears houses and an oil tempering building stand in blocks 171 to 173, and the rest is vacant. Monmouth Street is drawn as a creek running in the street bed and turning south along South 6th Street. A heavy frame at the lower right encloses an inset drawn on its own, which is not part of this description.
notes: Placed from two points carried from neighbouring sheets as a similarity (helmert): a lot corner at South 5th / Middlesex drawn on sheet 7, and the South 7th / Middlesex junction drawn on sheet 10. Low confidence; the neighbours' own placements are extrapolated at these corners, and a third estimate (sheet 10 at South 5th / Middlesex) differs by about 4 m.
The area is redeveloped (Red Bull Arena and new streets); Somerset, Hunterdon, Burlington and Monmouth Streets do not survive here, and South 7th Street does not reach this far.
Middlesex Street is today Angelo Cifelli Drive.

50 ft, north up (unlike sheets 7, 8, 10). Part 1: Crucible Steel Co. of America, Atha Works, S. 5th to S. 7th Sts, Middlesex to Monmouth (redeveloped, Red Bull Arena area); no surviving junction, placed from two points carried from sheets 7 and 10 (helmert, low confidence). Part 2: inset at lower right (open hearth furnace building, S. 6th St, Salem St, creek): unplaced.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset at lower right: open hearth furnace building and siding on S. 6th St at Salem St, beside a creek (Crucible Steel works) (no street junction survives; the inset's location relative to the main map is not drawn and the area is redeveloped; needs a feature shared with a placed sheet, or a surveyed point on the old S. 6th St / Salem St line).

sheet-10.description: Sheet 10 shows the south-western corner of Harrison, from South 5th Street at the top through South 6th Street to South 7th Street at the bottom, with north toward the right. Middlesex, Railroad Avenue, Essex, Bergen and Sussex Streets cross it, with Essex and Bergen marked 60 feet wide. At the left, the Pennsylvania Railroad main line and the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad lie on both sides of Railroad Avenue and cut off triangular lots in blocks 153, 168 and 169. A cluster of frame dwellings, flats, a hall and a saloon stands on block 153. Blocks 154 and 167 are open ground between the tracks and Essex Street. Block 155 has dwellings and flats along its east side, with a carriage shop, and block 166 is mostly vacant. At the right, the General Electric Company occupies block 156 with iron-clad and fire-proof reinforced concrete buildings, and carries a note to see sheet 8. Block 165 below it holds rows of dwellings and flats on Bergen Street and Sussex Street. A compass rose lies at the left in Railroad Avenue and the scale bar at the bottom. The sheet numbers 8, 9, 12 and 13 are printed in the margins for neighbouring sheets.
notes: Middlesex is today's Angelo Cifelli Drive; Railroad Avenue is New Jersey Railroad Avenue; South 6th Street is 6th Street in OpenStreetMap.
Bergen Street and South 7th Street junction was left out: the detector paired a lot line with the street edge (narrow pair, 2.6 m).
Control covers the eastern half; the left side beyond Railroad Avenue has none.
General Electric Company is the firm drawn on blocks 130 and 131 of sheet 8.
50 ft, north to the right. S. 5th to S. 7th Sts, Middlesex to Sussex; General Electric, DL&W and PRR tracks. Left half (Middlesex, Railroad Av) without control.

sheet-11.description: Sheet 11 covers the residential blocks of central Harrison between South 3rd Street at the top and South 5th Street at the bottom, with Sussex Street at the left edge, Warren Street and Jersey Street running between the blocks, Ann Street to the right, and Harrison Avenue along the right-hand side. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and is turned so that north points toward the right of the page. South 4th Street and Lodi Street divide the sheet into rows of blocks numbered 122 to 129. Nearly all the buildings are small frame dwellings with a few flats, stores and sheds, packed along the street frontages of narrow lots, while the lower blocks toward Ann Street and Harrison Avenue are largely empty subdivisions with lot lines drawn but few buildings. Harrison Avenue is lined with stores, real estate offices, a bank, saloons and a bakery. The most prominent buildings are the Holy Cross Church, with its school house and a parish hall, and, lower down, Davis Memorial M. E. Church with a spire, near a compass rose in the margin. A hose company house, marked Hose Co. No. 3, stands at the lower left, and Gus Baudendistel's herring pickling works with an auto repairing shop stands at the foot of the sheet near South 5th Street. Water pipes of 6 and 10 inches are drawn in the streets, a fire alarm box is marked on Harrison Avenue, and street widths of 50, 60 and 66 feet are lettered. Sheets 8, 12 and 19 adjoin, and a scale of feet is printed at the bottom.
notes: South 4th Street is today's Frank E. Rodgers Boulevard South.
Lodi Street is not in the modern street network.
Ann Street / South 5th Street and South 5th Street / Sussex Street were not detected.
The sheet is turned with north to the right (rotation about 92 degrees).
50 ft, north to the right. S. 3rd to S. 5th Sts, Sussex to Harrison Av; Holy Cross Church.

sheet-12.description: Sheet 12 covers a district of central Harrison between Harrison Avenue along the top and Sussex Street along the bottom, and between South 5th Street on the left and South 7th Street on the right, with Washington Street and South 6th Street running down the sheet and Ann, Jersey, Warren and Wilhelm streets crossing it. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the top, tilted slightly to the left, and a compass rose stands in the left margin. The blocks are numbered 157 to 164. Harrison Avenue is the commercial edge, with a row of frame stores, a bakery with an oven under the ground, saloons and a blacksmith shop, and W. F. Wiedener's carriage and wagon manufactory stands in Washington Street. Washington Street School No. 1, a large brick building with a stairway, sits in the block to the left of Washington Street, and the German Lutheran Church lies between Ann and Jersey streets toward the right. The blocks between are filled with small frame dwellings on narrow lots, with a few flats, a carpenter shop and a tinsmith and plumber's shop. Block 157 in the lower left is drawn at a different angle from its neighbours, its lots fanning out around Warren Street, and several blocks near South 7th Street, Jersey and Wilhelm streets are laid out in lots with almost no buildings. Water pipes of 6 inches run in the streets, street widths of 50, 60 and 66 feet are lettered, and the lower left carries a scale of feet. Sheets 10, 11 and 14 adjoin.
notes: South 6th Street is today's 6th Street (and South 6th Street at Wilhelm Street).
South 7th Street / Wilhelm Street was left out of the control because South 7th bends there.
Ann Street / South 5th Street, Jersey Street / South 5th Street, 6th Street / Sussex Street, South 7th Street / Sussex Street and Harrison Avenue / South 7th Street were not detected.
50 ft, north up. Harrison Av to Sussex, S. 5th to S. 7th Sts; Washington St School No. 1.

sheet-13.description: Sheet 13 covers the southeastern corner of Harrison, a thinly built district of large blocks and railroad land between South 7th Street at the top and Worthington Avenue along the bottom. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and is turned so that north points toward the right of the page. Bergen, Sussex and Wilhelm streets run down the sheet, with Manor Avenue crossing them diagonally in the middle. A wide fan of tracks of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad fills the left margin. Most of the sheet is blank: two very large undivided blocks, numbered 189 and 189 1/2, occupy the upper half beside a compass rose, with nothing built on them, and lots are laid out but unbuilt in blocks 201 to 204 below Manor Avenue and beside Wilhelm Street. The few buildings are the National Hoisting Engine Company's machine and erecting shop with its storage sheds and pattern storage, which has its own printed note on watchman, clock, stations and fire apparatus, a short row of lettered frame dwellings and a saloon on the south side of Manor Avenue near Bergen Street, and a vacant works with a tall chimney and a fire alarm box on the south side of block 203. Water pipes of 6 and 10 inches run in the streets, with hydrants and tap houses marked, and street widths of 50 and 60 feet are lettered. Bergen Street and Essex Street are named in the top margin where they continue onto sheet 10. Sheets 10, 12, 14 and 16 adjoin, and a scale of feet is printed at the lower right.
notes: Worthington Avenue is today's Supor Boulevard.

The sheet is placed from four hand-picked junctions (Manor Avenue and Worthington Avenue with Sussex and Wilhelm streets); Bergen Street and South 7th Street junctions were left out because their modern positions do not match the drawn ones.
The sheet is turned with north to the right (rotation about 94 degrees).
50 ft, north to the right. S. 7th St to Worthington Av (Supor Blvd), Bergen to Wilhelm; National Hoisting Engine Co.; mostly blank blocks; placed from 4 hand-picked junctions.

sheet-14.description: Sheet 14 covers four residential blocks in the eastern part of Harrison, bounded by Harrison Avenue on the north, Wilhelm Street on the south, South 7th Street on the west and Worthington Avenue on the east, with Manor Avenue dividing the blocks north to south and Ann, Jersey and Warren streets crossing them. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the top. The district was only partly built in 1907: most lots are drawn as empty subdivisions, and the buildings are concentrated along Harrison Avenue and at the western ends of Ann, Warren and Jersey streets. They are mostly frame dwellings and flats with a few stores and saloons, among them a row of flats on the north side of Ann Street and a restaurant and saloon on Wilhelm Street near Worthington Avenue. The one commercial establishment of size is W. W. Snyder's lumber, brick and cement yard, with sheds, a tool house and several lumber piles, on the south side of Jersey Street just east of South 7th Street. A fire alarm box stands on Harrison Avenue. Water pipes, mostly 6 and 8 inches, are drawn in Harrison Avenue, Ann Street and along South 7th Street, with hydrants at the corners. The edges of sheets 12, 13, 15, 20 and 21 are indicated in the margins, and the street widths are lettered in feet. The blocks are numbered 193 to 200.
notes: Worthington Avenue is today's Supor Boulevard.
South 7th Street bends at Wilhelm Street on the sheet; that junction was left out of the control.
W. W. Snyder lumber, brick and cement yard on Jersey Street.
50 ft, north up (pilot). Harrison Av to Wilhelm, S. 7th St to Worthington Av (now Supor Blvd), Manor Av; W.W. Snyder lumber yard.

sheet-15.description: Sheet 15 shows the eastern edge of Harrison where it meets Kearny, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned on the page so that north points to the left. Harrison Avenue runs down the left edge and Worthington Avenue along the bottom; Ogden Avenue crosses the upper part diagonally and carries the dash-dot line of the boundary between the Town of Harrison and the Town of Kearny. North of Ogden Avenue the sheet shows partly built residential blocks along Ann and Jersey streets and Sandford Avenue, with dwellings, a few stores and a saloon, and an infant's cloak manufactory near Harrison Avenue. A strip of small lots with dwellings lies south of Ogden Avenue near Harrison Avenue. The rest of the sheet is taken up by the Henry R. Worthington Hydraulic Works, marked 'admittance refused', whose long brick shops with raised side lights fill the ground between Ogden Avenue and Worthington Avenue; the works continue on sheet 16. Short stubs of Ann, Jersey, Warren and Wilhelm streets are drawn below Worthington Avenue at the bottom edge, where sheet 14 begins, and Warren Street is lettered beyond Ogden Avenue in Kearny. A fire alarm box stands on Harrison Avenue, and water pipes are drawn in Harrison, Ogden and Worthington avenues. Blocks 226 to 228 are numbered on the sheet.
notes: Worthington Avenue is today's Supor Boulevard; Sandford Avenue is Sanford Avenue.
Ann Street / Ogden Avenue was hand-picked: the detector paired a lot line.
Henry R. Worthington Hydraulic Works ('admittance refused').
50 ft, turned (north left). Harrison Av, Ogden Av (Harrison/Kearny boundary), Ann, Sandford Av, Worthington Av; Henry R. Worthington Hydraulic Works.

sheet-16.description: Sheet 16 continues the Henry R. Worthington Hydraulic Works from sheet 15 at the eastern edge of Harrison. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned so that north points to the left. Worthington Avenue runs along the bottom edge, with the stubs of Wilhelm, Sussex and Bergen streets drawn below it, and Ogden Avenue crosses the upper left corner, where the boundary between the Town of Kearny and the Town of Harrison follows it and short lengths of Warren, Wilhelm and Sussex streets are drawn beyond it. Almost the whole sheet is the works: long brick shop buildings with raised side lights, including an L-shaped block and a separate shop, set in otherwise empty ground marked 'admittance refused'. Along the right edge the many tracks of the Pennsylvania Railroad yard curve across the sheet, with a trolley line beside them. Beyond the works the sheet shows no streets or dwellings. Water pipes are drawn in Worthington Avenue with hydrants at the street ends, and blocks 224 and 225 are numbered. The pink of the works buildings continues across the left edge from sheet 15.
notes: Worthington Avenue is today's Supor Boulevard.
Placed from three hand-picked junctions along Worthington Avenue only (helmert); low confidence.
Pennsylvania Railroad yard along the right edge.

50 ft, turned (north left). Worthington Hydraulic Works east of sheet 15; Worthington Av along the bottom, Ogden Av corner, Penna RR yard on the right. Only junctions: three stubs on Worthington Av (helmert).

sheet-17.description: Sheet 17 covers the Passaic River waterfront of northern Harrison, from the town boundary with East Newark at the left to Harrison Avenue at the right, and from John Street at the top down to the river bank at the bottom, with Passaic Avenue running along the foot of the blocks. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and is turned so that north lies toward the left of the page. Hamilton Street and Cleveland Avenue run down the sheet between blocks of small frame dwellings, tenements, flats, saloons and stores, the densest frontage lying along Harrison Avenue where J. J. Mulligan and Sons' coal yard, a gospel mission, a tin shop and a hay and grain store are lettered. The tracks of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad sweep across the sheet in a wide curve on a concrete retaining wall. Industry fills the strip between Passaic Avenue and the river: Carr and Ball's stone works, Durie and Davidson's stone works, S. M. Clark's cooperage, the Federal Wire Cloth Company's wire weaving mill and foundry, and David Harper's mason's materials yard with its stone pockets and track above, while P. Toohey and Sons' coal yard and the Binsse Machine Company's shops stand to the left of the tracks. The boundary of the Borough of East Newark and the Town of Harrison is lettered along the railroad. A fire alarm box stands at Harrison Avenue and Passaic Avenue, water pipes are drawn in the streets, and a compass rose and a scale of feet are printed in the margins. The blocks are numbered 1 to 4 and the neighbouring sheets 6, 10 and 28 are marked at the edges.
notes: The Binsse Machine Company stands on the East Newark side of the boundary at the left edge.
Sheet turned with north to the left (rotation about -80 degrees).
Dey Street and New Street are not in the modern street network at this position.

50 ft, north to the left. Passaic River waterfront, John St to Harrison Av, Hamilton to Passaic Av; Federal Wire Cloth Co., Binsse Machine Co., Carr & Ball stone works. Five points, none west of the railroad.

sheet-18.description: Sheet 18 covers the north end of central Harrison between William Street at the top and Harrison Avenue along the bottom, with John Street on the left and North 3rd Street on the right. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the top, tilted slightly to the left, and a compass rose stands at the top right. Hamilton Street and Cleveland Avenue cross the sheet from left to right, and North 2nd Street runs down the middle, in two pieces that meet at a bend near the upper left. The upper left of the sheet is a wedge of long blocks turned to follow John Street and William Street, filled with frame dwellings and flats on narrow lots, with a fire alarm box at the top. Below them the blocks numbered 12 to 15 are drawn square to Hamilton Street, Cleveland Avenue and Harrison Avenue. Most buildings are two and three storey frame dwellings, flats and tenements, but Harrison Avenue is a commercial street of three-storey stores, among them a saloon, undertaker, drug store, hardware and meat stores, a barber, a tailor and a bicycle shop. Hamilton Street School No. 2, a brick school with two chimneys, stands on Hamilton Street, and the Cleveland Avenue Synagogue stands on Cleveland Avenue; a sausage-making works is marked in block 14. Water pipes of 6 and 10 inches run in the streets, with hydrants, and street widths of 50 and 60 feet are lettered. Sheets 17, 19, 28, 30 and 6 are indicated at the edges, a scale of feet is printed at the bottom, and a Library of Congress map division stamp appears at the foot.
notes: North 2nd Street continues south of Harrison Avenue as Economy Supply Way in the modern street network.
John Street here is the modern John Street at its Hamilton Street and William Street junctions.
Economy Supply Way / North 2nd Street and Cleveland Avenue / Economy Supply Way were not detected.
50 ft, north up. William St to Harrison Av, John to N. 3rd St.

sheet-19.description: Sheet 19 covers a district of Harrison between North 3rd Street on the south and North 5th Street on the north, from Cross Street on one side to Harrison Avenue on the other, in six columns of blocks cut by William, Hamilton and Cleveland streets and North 4th Street. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the left of the sheet, so the streets named for numbers run across the page. The blocks are almost solidly built with frame dwellings of two and a half stories and flats, most on narrow deep lots with sheds and stables behind. The civic and institutional buildings stand in the lower right: the City Hall, with Neptune Hose Co. No. 2 and Harrison Truck Co. No. 1 (hook and ladder) beside it, a bell and hose tower, an ambulance house and a fire alarm box, on Harrison Avenue at North 4th Street. Public School No. 3 stands at the upper left near Cross Street, a First Baptist Church and Christ Church are drawn on the blocks near North 4th Street, and J. J. Mulligan and Sons' coal yard lies beside City Hall. Along Harrison Avenue are stores, saloons, a laundry, a tailor, an undertaker, a barber, a florist with greenhouse, a harness maker and the Security Storage Warehouse, a fireproof concrete building. The Record Building (printing) is also drawn here. Water pipes of 6, 10, 12 and 14 inches are shown in the streets, with hydrants at corners and dimensions of street widths of 50, 60 and 66 feet. Adjoining sheets 18, 20, 29 to 33 are indicated in the margins.
notes: North 4th Street is today's Frank E. Rodgers Boulevard North.
The street named Hamilton is today's Hamilton Street, and William and Cross are today's William Street and Cross Street.
Cross Street / North 3rd Street was left out of the control (3.6 m residual, drawn at the sheet edge).
The compass shows north toward the left of the sheet.
50 ft, north to the left. North 3rd to North 5th Sts, Cross St to Harrison Av (City Hall, Public School No. 3).

sheet-20.description: Sheet 20 shows the part of Harrison between Davis Avenue and North 5th Street, with Patterson Street crossing the middle, and from Cross Street on one side to Harrison Avenue on the other. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the left. The upper third is mostly blank paper and a large block lettered 43 bounded by Hiram Avenue, which holds a single dwelling and outbuildings (a storage building, a crib, a coop, a servants' house) on a large lot. Below Davis Avenue the blocks are filled with frame dwellings and flats, with some irregular lots cut by diagonal lines. The sheet's main works are in the lower right block: Peter Hauck and Co., Brewers, with a brewhouse, fireproof filling room, storage, fermenting and cooling floors, wash house, malt bins, bottling department, ice machine and ammonia condenser rooms, and bar fixture storage, with a note on its fire protection (two Worthington fire pumps, water tanks, 12 chemical extinguishers). Other works are the Globe Wire Co. and The Hall Manufacturing Co., makers of engineers' supplies, with a brass foundry and machine shop that was not yet in operation. A club room and billiard room stand on Patterson Street, and saloons and a hall appear along Harrison Avenue. Water pipes of 6, 8 and 10 inches are drawn in the streets. The edges of sheets 12, 14, 19, 21, 33, 34, 35 and 36 are shown in the margins.
notes: The street printed Patterson is today's Patterson Street.
Hiram Avenue is today's Hiram Place.
The compass shows north toward the left of the sheet.
The upper part of the sheet is the edge of the district shown on sheet 21 and is largely blank.
50 ft, north to the left. Davis Av to North 5th St, Cross to Harrison Av (Peter Hauck and Co. brewery); top third nearly blank.

sheet-21.description: Sheet 21 shows a strip of Harrison lying between Worthington Avenue on one edge and Davis Avenue on the other, from Cross Street across William, Hamilton and Cleveland streets to Harrison Avenue. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the left, so the long blocks run across the page. Most of the area was subdivided but not built up in 1907: the upper two thirds of each block is a field of narrow lots drawn as bare parcels, and the buildings are found only near Davis Avenue, mainly frame dwellings of two and a half stories with sheds, and a row of flats and houses on the west side of Cross and William streets. The one large establishment is the Harrison branch car barns of the Public Service Corporation of New Jersey, on the Cleveland Avenue block beside Harrison Avenue, with a long car barn, repair shop, wash house, sand and soap house, air compressing house, electric motor room and office, and a note on watchman, power, heating and fire apparatus. A diagonal line crosses the block between Hamilton and Cleveland streets. Hiram Avenue runs between the car barns and the block lettered 20 to the south, which belongs to sheet 20. Water pipes of 4, 6, 8 and 10 inches are drawn in the streets, and street widths of 60, 70 and 80 feet are lettered.
notes: Worthington Avenue north of Harrison Avenue is today's Kingsland Avenue.
Hiram Avenue is today's Hiram Place.
The compass shows north toward the left of the sheet.
Control rests on Hiram Place and Davis Avenue and on Kingsland Avenue; the middle of the sheet has no junction.
50 ft, north to the left. Worthington Av (Kingsland Av north of Harrison Av) to Davis Av, mostly unbuilt lots; Public Service car barns.

sheet-22.description: Sheet 22 covers the north-east corner of Harrison beside the Kearny line, between Worthington Avenue on the west and Schuyler Avenue, which here follows the boundary of the towns of Harrison and Kearny, on the east, and from Harrison Avenue at the foot of the sheet up to the Erie Railroad at the top. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the top, and the grid is turned about 10 degrees. Hamilton Street crosses the sheet in the middle and Cleveland Avenue enters from the west as a stub. The upper half is industrial: the New Jersey Tube Co. rolling mill with its shipping, drawing, rod, rolling, casting, brazing and steel tube departments occupies the upper left, and T. Shriver and Co., manufacturers of iron castings, has a large iron foundry and machine shop set diagonally between the tube works and the railroad, with a spur from the Erie Railroad (Newark and Paterson Branch) and notes on power, watchmen and fire apparatus. Two rows of greenhouses, lettered as to be moved, stand east of the foundry. South of Hamilton Street the blocks are mostly unbuilt lots with greenhouses of R. A. Duke, gardener, and others, and a few dwellings near Harrison Avenue. The sheet shows water pipes of 3, 4, 6, 8 and 10 inches and street widths of 50, 60, 66, 70 and 90 feet. The edges of sheets 15, 21 and 23 are indicated.
notes: Worthington Avenue is today's Kingsland Avenue north of Harrison Avenue.
The street printed Franklyn is today's Franklin Avenue (Kearny).
Only five junctions were measured and the leave-one-out error is about 3 m.
Schuyler Avenue forms the town line between Harrison and Kearny.
50 ft, north up. NE Harrison at the Kearny line, Worthington to Schuyler Avs: New Jersey Tube Co., T. Shriver and Co., greenhouses. Five points, all south of Hamilton St.

sheet-33.description: Sheet 33 shows the boundary between Harrison and East Newark, between North 5th Street at the top and North 3rd Street at the foot, and from Hill Street across Davis Street and Central Avenue to Cross Street. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the left, so the lettered streets run up the page; Sherman Avenue and the Erie Railroad (Newark and Paterson Branch) run diagonally at the left, where the line between the Town of Harrison, the Town of Kearny and the Borough of East Newark is marked. The blocks are filled with frame dwellings of two and a half stories, flats and stores, with a row of saloons and shops along North 4th Street east of Central Avenue and a bakery, laundry and barber on the south side. The East Newark public school stands at the lower middle on a plot cut by North 3rd Street, which here runs diagonally. Industrial buildings are the Terrance Mfg. Co. near Hill Street and the Greenfield Steam Engine Works at the upper right on North 5th Street. The Board of Health office, a dance hall, a post office and a carpenter shop are also drawn. Water pipes of 6, 14, 16, 20 and 30 inches are shown, the larger being mains of the Suburban Water Co. The edges of sheets 19, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 30, 32, 34 and 39 are lettered in the margins.
notes: North 4th Street is today's Frank E. Rodgers Boulevard North.
The streets printed Davis, Central Avenue and Cross are today's Davis Street, Central Avenue and Cross Street.
Hill is not in the modern street data.
Central Avenue / Frank E. Rodgers Boulevard North was left out (11 m off the drawn junction).
The compass shows north toward the left of the sheet.
50 ft, north to the left. Harrison / East Newark line, North 3rd to North 5th St, Hill to Cross.

sheet-34.description: Sheet 34 covers the area of Harrison and Kearny where the Erie Railroad (Newark and Paterson Branch) passes between Central Avenue and the freight tracks, between North 5th Street on the west and Davis Avenue on the east, with Cross Street along the foot of the sheet. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the top and the grid turned about 4 degrees. The largest feature is the American Radiator Co. plant beside the railroad, an iron-clad storage and shipping building with an office and a separate iron-clad storehouse west of it, with elevated platforms along the track and a switch tower at the right edge. South of the plant the blocks along Central Avenue and Cross Street are small lots with frame dwellings, flats and stores, including the Harrison Baptist Church, a saloon and a barber. At the upper left the sheet reaches into Kearny, where a short row of dwellings stands between North 5th Street, Devon and Johnston Avenue, and F. Sommers' machine shop is shown on a lot to the east; the large blocks north of the tracks between Keasbey Street and Erie Avenue, with lot lines but almost no buildings, belong to Kearny. A diagonal line marks the boundary of the Town of Harrison and the Town of Kearny. Water pipes of 6 and 8 inches are drawn in the streets. The edges of sheets 20, 33, 36, 37, 38, 39 and 62 are indicated in the margins.
notes: The streets printed Davis, Central Avenue and Cross are today's Davis Street, Central Avenue and Cross Street; Davis Avenue is today's Davis Avenue.
Erie Avenue is not in the modern street data.
The upper part of the sheet (Keasbey Street, Erie Avenue) has no control point; the fit rests on the junctions along Central Avenue and Cross Street.
Davis Street / North 5th Street was picked by hand.
50 ft, north up. Erie RR, American Radiator Co., Central Av and Cross St; upper Kearny part (Keasbey, Erie Av, Devon) without control.
